metadata.title: AI Essentials
metadata.description: AI literacy for GSCM undergraduates: how models work, how to use them, and how to choose tools.

diagnostic.title: AI Essentials Placement Diagnostic
diagnostic.description: Quick check across practical AI fundamentals. Score at least 75% to place out of concepts you already know.

questions.prompt: Which is the best measure of value from an AI-assisted weekly operations report?
options: Number of prompts used
Time saved while verified report quality is maintained
Length of the generated report
How human the writing sounds
questions.answerKey: Time saved while verified report quality is maintained
questions.explanation: Measure an operational outcome with a quality check, not activity or novelty.

questions.prompt: What does a machine-learning model primarily do?
options: Applies only fixed rules written by a person
Learns patterns from examples to produce likely outputs
Guarantees every future prediction
Takes responsibility for decisions
questions.answerKey: Learns patterns from examples to produce likely outputs
questions.explanation: Machine learning learns patterns from data; outputs remain estimates that need appropriate evaluation.

questions.prompt: A model invents a shipment date that is not in any provided source. What is this?
options: A context window
A hallucination
A deterministic calculation
A guardrail
questions.answerKey: A hallucination
questions.explanation: A hallucination is a plausible but unsupported or false generated claim.

questions.prompt: Which prompt is most likely to produce a useful supplier update?
options: Make this better
Summarize logistics
Using the attached approved update, draft a 120-word note for the operations team with verified delays and next actions
Write anything about suppliers
questions.answerKey: Using the attached approved update, draft a 120-word note for the operations team with verified delays and next actions
questions.explanation: Useful prompts specify the source, task, audience, format, and factual constraints.

questions.prompt: What should guide model selection for a high-volume document classification task?
options: The largest model available
Quality on representative cases, latency, cost, and security requirements
The newest marketing announcement
Whether the model can produce long poems
questions.answerKey: Quality on representative cases, latency, cost, and security requirements
questions.explanation: Choose against the real task and operational constraints, not a general leaderboard.

questions.prompt: Which is a concrete guardrail for an AI purchasing assistant?
options: Tell it to be careful
Allow it to send orders without review
Use read-only data access and require approval before an external message
Remove audit logs
questions.answerKey: Use read-only data access and require approval before an external message
questions.explanation: Least-privilege access and approval gates directly limit risky actions and make them reviewable.

questions.prompt: Why connect a model to an approved inventory system instead of asking it to guess stock levels?
options: It makes the response more creative
The system can retrieve current records that can be checked
It removes the need for human review
It guarantees the business decision is correct
questions.answerKey: The system can retrieve current records that can be checked
questions.explanation: Grounding a response in an authorized system improves factual support, though decision review may still be required.

trackedDimensions.label: AI impact on work and life

lessons.title: AI in a GSCM Day
keyConcepts: AI impact on work and life

blocks.content: **AI is a workflow amplifier, not a substitute for judgment.** In supply chain work, it can summarize a supplier update, draft a demand-planning memo, and turn a meeting transcript into action items. You still own the facts, trade-offs, and decision.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain AI impact on work and life. Use one practical example.
evaluatesConcepts: AI impact on work and life

blocks.prompt: Put a responsible AI-assisted task workflow in order:
items: Define the business question and audience
Give the model relevant source material and constraints
Review claims against source data
Edit, approve, and send the deliverable

questions.prompt: Which task is the strongest first use of AI for a buyer?
options: Approve a supplier contract without reading it
Draft a comparison table from approved supplier quotes
Invent a new vendor score from no data
Replace the final negotiation decision
questions.answerKey: Draft a comparison table from approved supplier quotes
questions.explanation: AI can speed up structuring known information. Contract approval and negotiation accountability remain human responsibilities.

questions.prompt: A model summarizes a late-shipment report. What is the best next step?
options: Forward it immediately
Check the cited shipments and dates against the report
Assume the summary is correct because it is concise
Delete the original report
questions.answerKey: Check the cited shipments and dates against the report
questions.explanation: A useful output is a starting point. Verify important claims against the source before acting.

blocks.content: Practical habit: keep the original spreadsheet, email, or policy next to the draft. Ask AI to reduce clerical work; use your domain knowledge to make the call.

lessons.title: When AI Looks Like Magic
keyConcepts: AI impact on work and life

blocks.content: Modern AI can generate fluent text, images, code, and classifications because it learns patterns from large datasets. That capability can feel magical, but it does not guarantee understanding or accuracy.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain AI impact on work and life. Use one practical example.
evaluatesConcepts: AI impact on work and life

blocks.prompt: Order this demonstration from input to useful result:
items: Provide a clean inventory exception list
Ask for a manager-ready summary with defined columns
Receive a draft prioritized by stated rules
Validate the priority and share with the manager

questions.prompt: Why can a polished AI answer still be unsafe to use?
options: Fluent wording proves the model is correct
The model may generate plausible details not supported by evidence
AI can only repeat exact training sentences
Grammar errors are the only risk
questions.answerKey: The model may generate plausible details not supported by evidence
questions.explanation: Generative models can hallucinate: they may state unsupported or incorrect details confidently.

questions.prompt: What does pattern learning help a model do?
options: Guarantee the next quarter's demand
Recognize relationships in examples and generate likely outputs
Know facts it was never given
Accept legal responsibility for recommendations
questions.answerKey: Recognize relationships in examples and generate likely outputs
questions.explanation: Models estimate likely outputs from patterns. They do not guarantee future outcomes or take accountability.

blocks.content: The useful question is not "Is AI magic?" It is "What evidence would make this output trustworthy enough for this decision?"

lessons.title: Why This AI Wave Matters
keyConcepts: AI impact on work and life

blocks.content: Spreadsheets made calculation cheaper; the web made information easier to reach. Generative AI makes drafting, transforming, and interacting with information cheaper. The change matters when it reshapes a whole workflow, not when it creates a clever demo.

Past industrial revolutions lowered the cost of physical work, transportation, and calculation. This wave lowers the cost of some mental tasks. The comparison has limits: AI does not understand a workplace the way a colleague does, and adoption depends on data, process changes, trust, and accountability.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain AI impact on work and life. Use one practical example.
evaluatesConcepts: AI impact on work and life

blocks.prompt: Order these technology shifts from older to newer:
items: Spreadsheets automate calculations
The web broadens access to information
Cloud software connects shared workflows
Generative AI creates and transforms content from instructions

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes generative AI from a traditional spreadsheet formula?
options: Generative AI never needs inputs
A formula follows fixed logic; a generative model produces probabilistic output from instructions and context
Spreadsheets cannot support business decisions
Generative AI is always more accurate
questions.answerKey: A formula follows fixed logic; a generative model produces probabilistic output from instructions and context
questions.explanation: Formulas are deterministic when inputs are fixed. Generative outputs are probabilistic and require review.

questions.prompt: Where is the current AI wave most likely to create value?
options: Only in jobs that never use language
In workflows with repeated interpretation, drafting, search, or classification work
Only in tasks with no human owner
Only where errors have no cost
questions.answerKey: In workflows with repeated interpretation, drafting, search, or classification work
questions.explanation: AI is especially useful where teams repeatedly transform information, provided controls match the risk.

blocks.content: For GSCM, look for bottlenecks: reading exceptions, compiling updates, translating requirements, and preparing decisions. Measure time saved and error rate, not novelty.

lessons.title: Your AI Career Game Plan
keyConcepts: AI impact on work and life

blocks.content: AI raises the value of people who can frame a problem, supply context, test an answer, and coordinate action. Build a portfolio of repeatable workflows rather than collecting prompt tricks.

Efficiency can increase demand instead of reducing it. This is the Jevons paradox: when a resource becomes cheaper to use, people may use more of it. Cheaper analysis can mean more scenarios, more frequent forecasts, and higher expectations. Your advantage comes from deciding which extra work is worth doing.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain AI impact on work and life. Use one practical example.
evaluatesConcepts: AI impact on work and life

questions.prompt: A team uses AI to cut forecast preparation from two days to two hours, then starts updating forecasts weekly instead of monthly. What idea does this illustrate?
options: Lower cost can increase total use of a capability
Automation always reduces demand for work
Models become accurate when used more often
Forecasting no longer needs an owner
questions.answerKey: Lower cost can increase total use of a capability
questions.explanation: The cheaper workflow encouraged more frequent forecasting. That is the Jevons-style rebound effect.

blocks.prompt: Build an AI-ready work habit in order:
items: Choose one recurring low-risk task
Document the current time and quality baseline
Design and test an AI-assisted workflow
Keep the version that improves results with review

questions.prompt: Which is a safe student practice?
options: Paste confidential supplier pricing into a public tool
Use a course-approved tool with fictional or authorized data
Ask AI to fabricate citations
Submit AI output without reading it
questions.answerKey: Use a course-approved tool with fictional or authorized data
questions.explanation: Use approved tools and authorized data. Treat outputs as drafts you must understand and verify.

questions.prompt: Which skill remains most durable as AI tools change?
options: Memorizing one tool's button locations
Framing a business problem and evaluating evidence
Avoiding all automation
Copying the longest prompt online
questions.answerKey: Framing a business problem and evaluating evidence
questions.explanation: Problem framing and evidence-based judgment transfer across tools and models.

blocks.content: Start small: turn one weekly logistics update into a reviewed template. Record what AI did, what you checked, and where it failed. Keep practicing the underlying skill, too. If you outsource every calculation, summary, or first draft, your judgment can get rusty just as an unused muscle does.

lessons.title: Explain AI Models to a CEO
keyConcepts: AI impact on work and life

blocks.content: A model is a trained system that maps inputs to likely outputs. Explain it to a CEO as a capability with boundaries: "It can summarize approved documents and draft options, but it needs source access and human review for decisions."

During training, the model sees a corpus of examples and adjusts many numeric parameters to reduce prediction error. Backpropagation is the accounting mechanism for those adjustments: it traces how much each parameter contributed to an error, then nudges the parameters. It does not install a database of verified facts.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Machine learning basics. Use one practical example.
evaluatesConcepts: AI impact on work and life

questions.prompt: What does backpropagation do during model training?
options: Checks every statement against a trusted source
Adjusts parameters based on how they contributed to prediction error
Stores the training corpus as a searchable spreadsheet
Lets the model approve its own output
questions.answerKey: Adjusts parameters based on how they contributed to prediction error
questions.explanation: Backpropagation helps optimize parameters. Source quality and factual verification require separate controls.

blocks.prompt: Order the model lifecycle at a high level:
items: Collect and prepare training data
Train a model to learn patterns
Deploy the trained model for inference
Monitor output quality and update controls

questions.prompt: Which CEO explanation is most accurate?
options: The model knows everything on the internet
The model predicts useful outputs from patterns and supplied context
The model replaces every analyst
The model guarantees factual answers
questions.answerKey: The model predicts useful outputs from patterns and supplied context
questions.explanation: A model generates or classifies based on learned patterns and the context it receives; it is not a guaranteed source of truth.

questions.prompt: What business metric best supports an AI pilot?
options: Number of prompts written
Reduction in report-preparation time while maintaining verified accuracy
How impressive the demo sounds
Number of models purchased
questions.answerKey: Reduction in report-preparation time while maintaining verified accuracy
questions.explanation: A pilot should demonstrate an operational outcome with a quality control, not merely activity.

blocks.content: Good executive communication names the task, the data boundary, the owner, the expected benefit, and the failure mode.

An expert system applies explicit rules written by people: IF temperature is below a threshold, flag a cold-chain exception. Machine learning learns a pattern from examples: given past shipments, estimate which are likely to arrive late.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Expert systems. Use one practical example.
Classify the development sequence for a rule-based system:
items: Interview subject-matter experts
Write explicit if/then rules
Test edge cases
Deploy and revise rules when policy changes

questions.prompt: Which task is a strong fit for an expert system?
options: Apply a published compliance rule to every order
Write a nuanced supplier relationship summary
Generate several creative campaign ideas
Predict an unknown demand pattern from history
questions.answerKey: Apply a published compliance rule to every order
questions.explanation: Explicit, stable rules are transparent and auditable, which suits policy and compliance checks.

questions.prompt: Which task is a strong fit for machine learning?
options: Enforce a fixed minimum-order policy
Estimate delivery-delay risk from historical shipment features
Guarantee a factual policy answer
Replace a formal approval workflow
questions.answerKey: Estimate delivery-delay risk from historical shipment features
questions.explanation: Machine learning is valuable when examples contain predictive patterns that are difficult to hand-code.

blocks.content: Use rules when requirements are clear and traceability matters. Use ML when patterns are complex and you have representative data plus monitoring.
A language model generates the next likely token, not a signed statement of fact. It can help synthesize evidence, but it cannot turn missing, stale, or conflicting evidence into truth.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Machine learning basics. Use one practical example.
Order a fact-check loop for an AI-generated supplier brief:
items: Mark the claims that drive a decision
Open the source documents or system records
Correct unsupported claims and add citations
Approve the brief only after review

questions.prompt: What is a hallucination?
options: A verified answer with a citation
A plausible but unsupported or false generated claim
A faster search result
A rule-based validation
questions.answerKey: A plausible but unsupported or false generated claim
questions.explanation: Hallucinations are generated content that sounds credible but is not grounded in reliable evidence.

questions.prompt: A model gives different wording when asked the same question twice. What does that indicate?
options: It is necessarily broken
Generative outputs can vary because they are probabilistic
The source data changed automatically
All answers are false
questions.answerKey: Generative outputs can vary because they are probabilistic
questions.explanation: Variation is normal for generative models. Control it with clear constraints, grounding, and review.

blocks.content: For high-stakes claims, require a source, a reviewer, and a path to correct the record. Confidence in tone is not evidence.

Training is the expensive process of learning parameters from examples. Inference is using the trained model to answer a new request. A model can fail because training data was weak, the prompt lacked context, or the task exceeds its capability.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Machine learning basics. Use one practical example.
Put these stages in order:
items: Examples are collected and prepared
The model is trained on patterns
A user submits a new request
The deployed model generates an inference

questions.prompt: Which is inference?
options: Adjusting model parameters using training examples
A planner asking a deployed model to summarize today's exception report
Writing the original labeling guidelines
Removing a biased training record
questions.answerKey: A planner asking a deployed model to summarize today's exception report
questions.explanation: Inference is the live use of a trained model on a new input.

questions.prompt: Which control most directly reduces damage from an uncertain model output?
options: Let the model take irreversible action automatically
Set review and escalation rules based on decision risk
Hide the output from users
Use a longer model name
questions.answerKey: Set review and escalation rules based on decision risk
questions.explanation: Risk-based human review and escalation limit the effect of errors before an action is taken.

blocks.content: Diagnose failures before switching models. Ask: was the source available, was the instruction clear, did the model have the right capability, and was there a review gate?
A strong prompt is a work brief: role, task, context, constraints, and output format. Start with a small real example, inspect the output, then revise one variable at a time.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Prompting and iteration. Use one practical example.
Order a practical prompt iteration:
items: State the task and success criteria
Add the relevant context and constraints
Review the first output against the criteria
Revise the instruction or example and retest

questions.prompt: Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable shipment update?
options: Tell me about logistics
Write an update
Using the attached exception list, draft a 100-word update for operations leaders: group by root cause, list only verified counts, and end with two actions
Make it better
questions.answerKey: Using the attached exception list, draft a 100-word update for operations leaders: group by root cause, list only verified counts, and end with two actions
questions.explanation: It defines source context, audience, length, structure, and a factual constraint.

questions.prompt: What should you do when a model lacks a needed fact?
options: Tell it to be more confident
Provide the approved source or ask it to state what information is missing
Ask it to invent a reasonable value
Remove all constraints
questions.answerKey: Provide the approved source or ask it to state what information is missing
questions.explanation: Grounding the task in source material or acknowledging missing information is safer than inviting invention.

blocks.content: Save prompts that work as templates, but keep the review checklist with them. A reusable prompt is a small process, not a magic phrase.

For a complex task, a model may need context and access to tools such as a document search, calculator, or inventory system. The model coordinates steps; tools retrieve data or perform reliable operations.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Reasoning and context. Use one practical example.
Order a grounded analysis workflow:
items: Receive the business question
Retrieve relevant approved records
Use a calculator or system tool for exact values
Draft an answer tied to the retrieved evidence

questions.prompt: Why give a model a calculator tool for a cost calculation?
options: It makes the model more creative
It reduces arithmetic errors and makes a deterministic operation reliable
It removes the need for inputs
It guarantees the right business assumption
questions.answerKey: It reduces arithmetic errors and makes a deterministic operation reliable
questions.explanation: A calculator can reliably execute arithmetic, but the user still must provide valid inputs and assumptions.

questions.prompt: What is the best use of context in a prompt?
options: Add unrelated text until the prompt is long
Supply the relevant policies, data, definitions, and audience needs
Hide the decision criteria
Replace verification
questions.answerKey: Supply the relevant policies, data, definitions, and audience needs
questions.explanation: Relevant context lets the model tailor the output; unrelated context can distract it and increase cost.

blocks.content: Separate thinking from authority: a model can propose a plan, but a system of record and a human owner should confirm facts and authorize changes.
A harness is the surrounding system that gives a model instructions, tools, memory, permissions, and checks. The model is only one component. Reliable outcomes come from the full workflow design.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Tools, skills, and harnesses. Use one practical example.
Order a controlled purchase-order exception workflow:
items: Classify the exception from authorized data
Retrieve the relevant policy
Draft a recommended next step
Route high-risk cases to a human approver

questions.prompt: Which is a guardrail in an AI workflow?
options: A vague instruction to "be careful"
Restricting the model to read-only access and requiring approval before sending a supplier message
Giving it more unrelated documents
Removing audit logs
questions.answerKey: Restricting the model to read-only access and requiring approval before sending a supplier message
questions.explanation: Permissions and approval gates are concrete controls that limit what the system can do and make actions reviewable.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of tool permissions?
options: Make outputs sound more natural
Limit what data and actions the AI can access to what the task requires
Ensure every recommendation is correct
Avoid documenting the workflow
questions.answerKey: Limit what data and actions the AI can access to what the task requires
questions.explanation: Least-privilege access reduces exposure and the impact of tool misuse or model error.

blocks.content: Design the harness first: define the user, inputs, allowed tools, escalation path, audit trail, and owner. Then choose the model.

Model selection is not a leaderboard contest. Compare models by the task: quality, latency, cost, context capacity, tool use, privacy, and deployment constraints. A smaller model may be the best business choice.

The model zoo includes text-only and multimodal systems, open-weight models you can run yourself, and proprietary models accessed through a vendor. Aggregators provide one interface to several vendors. That can make switching easier, but it adds another provider to the security, reliability, and cost review.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Choosing AI models. Use one practical example.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team needs a model to interpret photos of damaged cartons alongside written notes. Which capability is required?
options: Text-only generation
Multimodal image and text input
A larger context window only
Speech synthesis
questions.answerKey: Multimodal image and text input
questions.explanation: The task combines images and text, so the evaluated model must support both modalities.

blocks.prompt: Order a model selection process:
items: Define the task and acceptance test
Shortlist models that meet security and deployment needs
Evaluate quality, speed, and cost on representative cases
Choose and monitor the model for the workflow

questions.prompt: A team needs fast classification of standard invoice fields at high volume. Which consideration is most important?
options: Only the largest model's benchmark score
Accuracy on representative invoices, latency, and cost per document
The model's marketing tagline
Whether it can write poetry
questions.answerKey: Accuracy on representative invoices, latency, and cost per document
questions.explanation: The selected model must meet the workflow's real quality, throughput, and cost requirements.

questions.prompt: When might a general model be a poor fit?
options: The task uses ordinary language
A specialized system already performs a narrow, regulated task more accurately and transparently
The team needs an API
A human will review the result
questions.answerKey: A specialized system already performs a narrow, regulated task more accurately and transparently
questions.explanation: Use the simplest system that meets the requirement. Specialized approaches can be better for narrow or regulated work.

blocks.content: Build a small evaluation set from realistic, authorized cases. Test before launch and keep it for regression checks when prompts or models change.

A context window is the amount of input and output a model can consider in one request. More context can help, but it also raises cost, latency, and distraction risk. Send the relevant slice, not every document.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Choosing AI models. Use one practical example.
Order a cost-conscious document workflow:
items: Identify the question to answer
Retrieve only relevant sections and metadata
Send the selected context with a structured instruction
Log quality, latency, and cost for review

questions.prompt: What is the most direct effect of sending much more text to a model?
options: It always improves accuracy
It can increase token cost and latency, and irrelevant material can distract the model
It eliminates the need for retrieval
It guarantees no hallucinations
questions.answerKey: It can increase token cost and latency, and irrelevant material can distract the model
questions.explanation: Longer inputs consume more tokens and can bury the evidence that matters.

questions.prompt: A 200-page supplier contract must be checked for one delivery clause. What is the best first step?
options: Paste the entire contract into every prompt
Retrieve the relevant clause and its surrounding definitions
Ask the model to guess the clause
Ignore the contract
questions.answerKey: Retrieve the relevant clause and its surrounding definitions
questions.explanation: Targeted retrieval gives the model the relevant evidence while controlling cost and attention.

blocks.content: Track cost per successful task, not only cost per token. An inexpensive answer that needs extensive rework is not economical.

A routing system directs each request to the right model, tool, or human queue. For example, a low-risk translation can use a fast model, while a contract exception goes to a stronger model and legal review.

Specialization has several forms. A system prompt sets behavior for the current application. Fine-tuning changes model weights using examples. Distillation trains a smaller model to imitate a stronger one, while quantization stores weights with less precision to reduce memory and compute. Start with prompting and retrieval; change the model only when evaluation shows a real gap.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Choosing AI models. Use one practical example.

questions.prompt: A team wants consistent answer structure but the base model already handles the task accurately. What should it try first?
options: A clear system prompt and evaluated examples
Training a foundation model from scratch
Quantization to change the writing style
Removing the evaluation set
questions.answerKey: A clear system prompt and evaluated examples
questions.explanation: Prompt-level controls are cheaper and easier to change. Fine-tuning is justified only when simpler controls fail an evaluated requirement.

blocks.prompt: Order a request-routing workflow:
items: Classify the request and risk level
Select the approved model, tool, or human queue
Process with the required controls
Log the result and route failures for review

questions.prompt: Why route simple tasks to a smaller model?
options: Smaller models are always more accurate
It can reduce cost and latency when the quality target is still met
It removes the need to test outputs
It makes policies unnecessary
questions.answerKey: It can reduce cost and latency when the quality target is still met
questions.explanation: Right-sizing models can preserve quality while reducing the operating cost of routine work.

questions.prompt: Which request should be routed to a human by default?
options: Formatting a public meeting agenda
Taking an irreversible action with significant financial or safety consequences
Summarizing an approved internal memo
Translating a non-sensitive draft
questions.answerKey: Taking an irreversible action with significant financial or safety consequences
questions.explanation: High-impact or irreversible decisions need human authority, even if AI prepares analysis.

blocks.content: Routing rules should be visible and testable: task category, sensitivity, risk, performance target, fallback, and accountable owner.

AI appears in several shapes: chat assistants, embedded copilots, search-and-answer systems, workflow automations, and agents that coordinate tools. Choose the shape that fits the job, not the flashiest interface.

The same feature can run in a vendor platform, inside an existing business application, in your cloud account, or on infrastructure you operate. The choice affects data residency, integration effort, updates, observability, and who responds when it fails. Put the feature where the required data and controls can be managed.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain AI systems beyond chatbots. Use one practical example.
Order these solutions from least to most workflow autonomy:
items: Chat assistant drafts a response
Copilot suggests text inside an application
Automation processes a defined trigger
Agent coordinates multiple tools within approved limits

questions.prompt: Which tool shape best fits a recurring weekly report assembled from the same approved systems?
options: A one-off image generator
A workflow automation with defined inputs, output template, and review step
An unrestricted agent with payment access
A manual copy-and-paste process only
questions.answerKey: A workflow automation with defined inputs, output template, and review step
questions.explanation: A repeatable process with stable inputs benefits from automation and an explicit review step.

questions.prompt: When is a chat assistant a good fit?
options: Exploring a question or drafting a first-pass outline with human review
Executing a supplier payment without approval
Replacing the system of record
Making a final legal interpretation
questions.answerKey: Exploring a question or drafting a first-pass outline with human review
questions.explanation: Chat is useful for interactive exploration and drafting, where the user can supply context and evaluate the response.

blocks.content: A useful design question: does this task need conversation, embedded assistance, deterministic automation, or controlled tool coordination?

Buy when a vendor product meets the need with acceptable security, integration, and total cost. Build when the workflow is distinctive enough to justify ongoing ownership of data pipelines, evaluation, monitoring, and support.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain AI systems beyond chatbots. Use one practical example.
Order a build-vs-buy decision:
items: Define the business outcome and constraints
Evaluate existing products against the requirements
Estimate integration and ongoing operating costs
Choose the option with the best total value and accountability

questions.prompt: Which cost is often missed when a team decides to build?
options: The ongoing cost of evaluation, monitoring, integration maintenance, and support
The color of the prototype
The number of prompt examples alone
The model name
questions.answerKey: The ongoing cost of evaluation, monitoring, integration maintenance, and support
questions.explanation: A custom AI system requires continuing work after launch: data quality, monitoring, security, support, and changes to models or policies.

questions.prompt: What should be checked before buying an AI vendor for sensitive operations data?
options: Only the product demo
Data handling, access controls, retention, contractual terms, integration, and audit needs
Whether the interface has animations
Whether it is the newest product
questions.answerKey: Data handling, access controls, retention, contractual terms, integration, and audit needs
questions.explanation: Sensitive data requires a complete risk and governance review, not just a feature comparison.

blocks.content: Do not build because AI is exciting. Build only where it creates differentiated value and you can own the operational responsibilities.

Safe deployment starts with a narrow use case, defined owner, authorized data, and measurable acceptance criteria. Expand only after testing real failure modes and documenting how users escalate problems.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain Safety and guardrails. Use one practical example.
Order a safe AI deployment:
items: Define scope, risk, owner, and success metric
Test representative cases and known failure modes
Launch with permissions, review gates, and monitoring
Review incidents and improve or limit the system

questions.prompt: A deployed assistant gives a confident but incorrect inventory policy answer. What should the system do?
options: Keep the answer because it sounded professional
Show the governing source, enable correction, and route the issue for review
Hide the incident from the owner
Automatically change the policy
questions.answerKey: Show the governing source, enable correction, and route the issue for review
questions.explanation: Grounding, correction paths, and incident review help contain and learn from incorrect outputs.

questions.prompt: Which deployment metric is most meaningful?
options: Total messages sent
Verified task success rate, error rate, escalation rate, and time saved
Number of emojis in outputs
Length of the system prompt
questions.answerKey: Verified task success rate, error rate, escalation rate, and time saved
questions.explanation: Operational metrics connect the deployment to quality, risk, and business value.

blocks.content: Treat deployment as a managed process. Monitor what the system does in practice, preserve an audit trail, and retain a human path for exceptions.

project.title: Build a trustworthy AI decision-support workflow
project.description: Design an AI-assisted workflow that turns a messy operational request into a reliable, evidence-backed recommendation. Show how a person frames the task, supplies context, uses tools, checks the output, handles failure, and makes the final decision.

deliverables.name: A one-paragraph use case, user, decision, and success definition
A reusable prompt with context, constraints, output format, and one documented iteration
A tool/harness plan showing inputs, steps, human checkpoints, and model choice
A guardrail and evaluation plan with at least three tests and a failure-response path
A final operating brief that explains what AI does, what the human owns, and why

milestones.name: Frame the decision and success criteria
milestones.checkDescription: Frame the decision and success criteria
